analytic.title: Interprocessor-Blocking Independent Static Task Allocation for Shared-Bus Real-Time Multiprocessors

div.p: In real-time systems, guaranteeing the schedulability of high priority tasks is more important than bezng able to schedule more tasks under resource constraints. The system bus in bus-based multiprocessors is a shared resource that is usually arbitrated b y priority and fairness. This paper presents a new static task allocation strategy that takes into consideration the impact of bus arbitration policy on schedulability. By allocafing task sets partitioned b y the descending order of priorities t o the processors in the order of physical priorities we can minimize the loss of schedulability caused by interference among processors. It is shown oia simulation that the proposed strategy keeps high priority tasks schedulable and reduces ihe schedulability loss up to 26% compared with the conventional allocation scheme.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The schedulability analysis of a real-time system needs to determine the worst case blocking time of each task. In a bus-based real-time multiprocessor environment, the worst case blocking time of a task consists of local blocking time and interprocessor blocking time. Local blocking of a task in a processor accounts for the time blocked by lower priority tasks in the processor and depends only on the characteristics of the task set associated with the processor. On the other hand, interprocessor blocking is the waiting time caused by interference among processors and depends on the characteristics of task sets allocated to other processors, bus arbitration policy and the hardwired priorities of processors during bus arbitration.

Interprocessor blocking makes the schedulability analysis difficult, and can make a locally schedulable Heonshik Shin and Yookun Cho Dept. of Computer Engineering Seoul National University Seoul 151-742, Korea processor unschedulable for the same task set. The bus arbitration policy decides which processor can be a bus master at any time and thus identifies the factors of interprocessor blocking. Although interprocessor blocking is conceptually similar to the remote blocking, the blocking factors are different from those of [l]. Furthermore, the impact of bus arbitration policy on schedulability has not been considered in the previous studies [l, 21. These problems motivate us to develop a new static task allocation strategy independent of interprocessor blocking. An appropriate task allocation taking the bus arbitration policy into account can keep the interprocessor blocking independent and the schedulability loss minimum.

In a bus-based multiprocessor environment , previous studies have dealt with the waiting time for each priority class to use bus for various bus arbitration mechanisms [6] and the priority management at the hardware transmission queue of the Bus Interface Unit(B1U) [4]. Real-time bus scheduling for a uniprocessor is analyzed in [5]. The task allocation for realtime multiprocessors, on the other hand, has focused on reducing the number of processors [l] and balancing the load over processors [7].

In this paper, we propose a static task allocation strategy in which high priority tasks are schedulable and low priority tasks always wait for high priority tasks. The basic idea of the proposed allocation strategy is to assign high priority tasks to processors with high geographical priorities. This assignment forces a processor with high priority tasks to always become the winner in the bus arbitration procedure. So the waiting time for high priority tasks to use the bus is reduced, thus minimizing the loss of schedulability due to inter processor blocking .

This paper consists of six sections. Section 2 describes the target system model and basic assumptions. Section 3 identifies the factors of interprocessor blocking. In Section 4, we describe, in detail, the proposed static task allocation strategy. Section 5 compares the performance of the proposed static task allocatmion scheme with that of conventional allocation for different memory request types by simulation. Concluding remarks and suggestions for further study are given in Section 6.

div.head: System Model
div.p: The target system is modeled as a bus-based realtime multiprocessor with shared memory as shown in Figure 1. Priority management a t the transmission queue and during bus arbitration process is an important issue related to the impact of a bus on schedulability. When more than one processor try to access the memory at the same time or at close intervals, a bus arbitration mechanism is used to select those requests which can be honored. The bus arbitration is based primarily on the priorities of the tasks bounded to a processor, and the geographical processor number for fairness when processors are competing with the same priority, such as Multibus [8] and Future-bus+ [9]. We ignore memory contention because our primary concern is with bus arbitration. Memory access time including bus arbitration time is assumed to be 100 nanoseconds for simplicity.

div.head: Interprocessor-Blocking Factors and Schedulability Analysis
div.p: Analyzing the schedulability of bus-based real-time multiprocessors requires that the blocking time Bi be known and divided into two components: Local blocking and interprocessor blocking, i.e., Bi =

Bi-rocai + Bi-intproc. Assuming that P r i is the priority of the task for which the worst case blocking time is calculated, Bi-local is computed as the sum of the memory access times of the tasks with priorities lower than Pri, i.e., when all tasks are placed by the as- cending order of priority a t the transmission queue.

BiintproC is a function of the distribution of priorities and memory request rate of tasks in other processors, and the bus arbitration policy used to select the bus master. A processor participating in the bus arbitration process with the priority inherited from its highest priority task dichotomizes the interprocessor blocking factors: Factor 1, for processors whose highest priority is higher than Pri, and Factor 2, for processors whose highest priority is the same as Pri. Factor 1 causes the worst case blocking time of Pri to be the sum of all memory accesses of all tasks assigned to the processor. This is because the inherited priority for arbitration competition is higher than Pri and the processor always becomes the bus master. The processor with P r i waits until the bus is free. Factor 2 causes the worst case blocking time of Pri to be the memory access time encountered among processors with P r i alternately by the fairness arbitration.

div.head: H
div.p: The proposed scheme forces low priority tasks to wait for higher priority tasks because the highest priority of the tasks allocated to a processor with a smaller processor number is always higher than the highest priority of the tasks allocated to a processor with a larger processor number. Hence the tasks in the processor with the highest physical priority do not experience interprocessor blocking. However, the tasks assigned to lower priority processors may experience delay due t o interprocessor blocking.

If the schedulability loss is reduced, more tasks are schedulable. For the task set in the example, the schedulability loss under the proposed task allocation scheme is reduced to 17.4% compared with the case of conventional allocation. The interprocessor blocking which makes high priority tasks unschedulable is es- timated to be about 65% of the total blocking in the conventional allocation.

Delay time at the transmission queues and waiting time for memory requests were obtained by simulation and they were used to calculate the blocking time in the average case. The simulation was performed using a simulator written in smpl [lo].

div.head: Results of Experiments
div.p: For analysis purpose, we investigate two cases depending on the memory request rate of each task. In the first case, the memory request rates of all the tasks are same. In the second case, tasks have different memory request rates. For each case, the comparison between the proposed allocation strategy and the conventional one is based on the number of schedulable tasks, which tasks are schedulable, and the schedulability loss. We concentrate on the advantage of the proposed static allocation over the conventional allocation in terms of schedulability.

Table 5 shows which tasks are schedulable for various memory request rates ranging from 5% to 15%. The table also shows the case where tasks have differ-ent memory request rates. In the table, HHLL corresponds to the case where high priority tasks have high have 15% memory request rates. It can be seen from Table 5 that as the memory request rate increases, the number of schedulable tasks decreases but most high priority tasks are schedulable in the proposed static allocation. However, in the case of conventional allocation, high priority tasks such as ~2 and r4 are unschedulable on the worst case whereas a lower priority task such as r 7 is schedulable. These trends are maintained for the HHLL and HLLH cases Figure 2 shows the schedulability losses (SL's) of the proposed static allocation and the conventional allocation when every task has the same memory request rate. The results were obtained assuming the blocking times calculated from simulat,ion (i.e., average case). The figure shows that the proposed allocation has lower SL's than the conventional allocation for all three cases. As expected, the SL increases as the memory request rate increases. However, the rate of increase is much lower in the proposed static allocation. This is due to the reduced interprocessor blocking in the proposed static allocation. Note that if we assumed the worst case instead, the conventional allocation would have yielded much worse schedulability loss.

div.head: Conclusion and Future Work
div.p: We have proposed a static task allocation strategy independent of interprocessor blocking in the sharedbus real-time multiprocessor environment. The key to the proposed scheme is the integration of bus arbitration policy into the task allocation to minimize the schedulability loss due to interprocessor blocking.
From experiments, we have shown that the proposed scheme reduces the schedulability loss and always forces high priority tasks to be schedulable.

There are several directions in which the work presented here can be extended. One such direction is to extend the priority management at the transmission queue to the priority overwrite which was proposed to eliminate local blocking.
